title: Stoics and Buddhists
hookLine: two calm schools that get mixed up online: what's in our power (Epictetus) and the second arrow (SN 36.6); similar practice, different reasons
tomorrow: the blind men and the elephant

cards: Two lines on a poster. One says it isn't things that upset us, but our opinions about them. The other says pain is one arrow, and we fire a second one into ourselves.
Which one is the Buddha? Online, they sometimes get swapped. The first is Epictetus, a Greek teacher who had once been enslaved in the Roman empire.
The second is the Buddha, in paraphrase. People keep asking whether Stoicism and Buddhism are the same thing. To close the right view week, an honest look.

teach.h: WHAT'S IN OUR POWER, AND WHAT ISN'T.
teach.b: Start with what's alike. Epictetus begins his handbook, in George Long's translation: "Of things some are in our power, and others are not." Our judgments, our wanting and not wanting, are ours.
The body, money, reputation, are not. Train yourself to tell the difference, and much of the distress falls away.
The Buddha's second arrow works the same ground. Someone untrained, struck by pain, adds worry and resistance on top: two arrows. Someone trained feels the first and doesn't fire the second.
Both schools watch their reactions closely.
Both reflect on death on purpose. Both prize a steady mind. That's why the comparison keeps coming up.
Now the difference, and it's in the reasons. The Stoics taught that the world is ordered by a divine reason, the logos, and the good life is living in agreement with it.
Virtue, they said, is the only true good, and your reasoning mind is the part that is really yours. The Buddha's teaching doesn't rest on a cosmic order.
It looks at what arises and passes, and turns the same look on the one doing the judging: is this me, is this mine? Its aim isn't agreement with nature. It's the end of craving.
Same calm on the surface, different roots underneath.
Neither needs the other to be wrong. And this week has been about exactly that: right view as a lens, not a trophy.
Seeing it is seeing, the truths closed, eight spokes, right view, roots, deeds that ripen, and today, two schools side by side.

how: Buddhist teachers who are asked about Stoicism often point to shared practices, watching reactions and reflecting on death, while noting that Buddhism grounds them in impermanence and not-self rather than in a reasoned cosmic order.

games.q: a friend says Buddhism is just Stoicism in a robe. what's the fairest reply?
games.why: both train reactions and remember death. the Stoics root it in a cosmic reason and the self's judgment; the Buddha, in seeing things arise and pass, including the judge.

practice: Bring to mind something small that's bothering you today. First, the Buddha's question: what is the first arrow here, the thing that actually happened, and what is the second, the part the mind keeps adding?
Then Epictetus's question: what here is in my power, and what isn't? Notice which question loosens something in you; there's no right answer, so just rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Stoicism. A Greek and Roman philosophy of calm through clear judgment: a neighbor to this path, with a similar practice and different reasons. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, not Pali: a porch. The Stoics are named for the Painted Porch in Athens, where Zeno of Citium taught.

carryVoice: Your line: same calm, different reasons. Two schools can look alike and still be two schools. Day three hundred fifty-seven.
